summary.overview: The poster presents a relevant, practice-oriented argument for integrating primary care into clinical-trial recruitment and offers a useful five-part operational framework. Its strong title, three-column organization, implementation example, conclusion, and references provide a recognizable narrative. However, the evidence-review method is not reported, several outcome claims are not quantified or clearly distinguished from proposed benefits, and extensive small text, dense diagrams, editing errors, and malformed references reduce readability and scientific credibility.
strengths: The central problem—fragmentation among sponsors, CROs, sites, primary care providers, and communities—is clearly identified.
The five-part practical framework translates the argument into concrete actions for clinical research professionals.
The PRACTICe example connects the proposed model to a named implementation setting and cites a source.
The poster includes a prominent title, author and affiliation, conclusion, in-text citations, and a reference section.
The three-column structure and repeated teal section bars create an overall left-to-right organization.
top_priorities: Add a concise methods/evidence-selection section and clearly distinguish literature-supported findings, PRACTICe process observations, and proposed recommendations.
Reduce the amount of prose and enlarge body, diagram, and reference text so the poster can be read comfortably at viewing distance.
Correct typographical, citation-numbering, bibliographic, and URL errors throughout the poster.
Revise the central and left-side graphics so each communicates one clear takeaway with fewer labels and a more obvious reading sequence.

findings.finding: The poster states that it draws on U.S. evidence and implementation models but does not explain how evidence or models were identified, selected, or synthesized.

evidence.description: The abstract says, “Drawing on U.S. evidence and implementation models,” and the practical framework says it is “Based on the evidence and implementation models reviewed,” but no search sources, inclusion criteria, review approach, date range, or synthesis method is shown.
evidence.section: Abstract; A Practical Framework for Clinical Research Professionals

findings.recommendation: Add a compact methods box specifying the review type, databases or source channels, search period, eligibility criteria, number and types of sources included, and how themes or framework elements were derived. If this was a narrative rather than systematic review, label it explicitly.

findings.finding: Several statements imply demonstrated effectiveness or scalability without showing the supporting measurements or clearly qualifying the level of evidence.

evidence.description: The PRACTICe section says early outcomes show improved workflow alignment, clearer priorities, strengthened trust, and that the approach is “feasible and scalable.” Elsewhere, the poster states that primary-care integration can improve awareness, retention, efficiency, and data quality, but no measures, comparison, time frame, or effect estimates are presented.
evidence.section: PRACTICe; Implications for Trial Diversity, Trust, and Efficiency

findings.recommendation: Separate observed process findings from hypothesized or literature-supported benefits. For each claimed outcome, identify the evidence source and whether it was measured, perceived, or proposed; soften causal or scalability language where supporting evaluation is preliminary.

findings.finding: The poster reports “early process outcomes” but provides no quantitative or structured qualitative evidence with which readers can assess those outcomes.

evidence.description: The PRACTICe description lists sustainable engagement infrastructure, improved workflow alignment, clearer research priorities, and strengthened trust without sample size, number of participating clinics or regions, data-collection method, indicators, baseline, follow-up period, or uncertainty. No statistical table or chart is present.
evidence.section: Primary Care Rural and Frontier Clinical Trials Innovation Center (PRACTICe)

findings.recommendation: If evaluation data are available, report the relevant denominators, time period, measures, and descriptive results, with uncertainty where appropriate. If they are not available, label these as preliminary process observations and describe how they were assessed rather than implying quantified outcome evidence.

findings.finding: The poster contains too much continuous prose and very small text for a 48-by-36-inch poster, especially in the abstract, background, case-study, conclusion, and references.

evidence.description: Large paragraph blocks span most of each 15–16-inch column, and the reference list compresses 15 sources into approximately the bottom five inches of the right column. The rendered poster shows that much of the body and reference text is difficult to read at overview scale.

findings.recommendation: Cut repeated explanation, convert paragraphs to short bullets, retain only evidence needed to support the central argument, and use body text of at least 24 points. Move full references or supplementary detail to a QR-linked document if allowed, while retaining essential citations on the poster.

findings.finding: Long and complex sentences obscure the main claims and repeat similar ideas across sections.

evidence.description: The abstract, fragmentation discussion, PRACTICe description, and conclusion use long multi-clause sentences. The consequences of fragmentation—slower enrollment, increased costs, and inequity—are repeated in blocks 5, 47, and 50.
evidence.section: Abstract; Why Diversity Goals Stall; PRACTICe; Conclusion

findings.recommendation: Use short, active statements organized as problem, evidence, intervention, and outcome. Remove repeated claims and visually emphasize one central takeaway plus three to five supporting points.

findings.finding: The poster has a recognizable column structure, but competing headings, dense content, and limited whitespace weaken the visual hierarchy and make the intended reading sequence less immediate.

evidence.description: Twelve extracted headings and 119 content blocks occupy nearly the full page. The left column contains a dense stakeholder matrix, the center includes multiple diagrams and labels, and the right column contains several similarly weighted text sections. The large “Primary Care > Research -> Equity” banner competes with the main title and adjacent section headings.

findings.recommendation: Create a more explicit top-to-bottom sequence within each column, reduce the number of heading levels, enlarge the primary takeaway, and introduce more whitespace between major sections. Numbering the three main stages—problem, model, action—would help guide readers.

guidance.section: Best Practices for an Effective Poster

findings.finding: The main graphics contain many small labels and do not communicate a single takeaway quickly.

evidence.description: The left ecosystem graphic distributes incentives, barriers, and impacts across five narrow stakeholder columns, while the center combines a segmented circle, multiple surrounding boxes, arrows, and a separate operational-model panel. At rendered overview size, the labels are visually subordinate and the relationship among components is difficult to infer rapidly.
evidence.section: Operational Fragmentation Across Clinical Research Ecosystem; Core Operational Elements of Silo-Bridging

findings.recommendation: Redesign each graphic around one declarative takeaway. Reduce labels, group related items, use larger type, and add a short caption that states what the reader should conclude. Consider replacing the segmented circle with a simpler process flow linking primary care integration to specific operational outcomes.

guidance.section: Best Practices for an Effective Poster

findings.finding: Numerous typographical, spacing, punctuation, and wording errors interrupt reading and create ambiguity.

evidence.description: Visible examples include “across stakeholder contribute,” “CROS,” “Administrativ e and documentati on burden,” “Across Successful,” “Practice -based,” “Closed -loop,” “late- stage,” missing spaces after numbered items, and bullets running together in “Improve awareness… .Reduce logistical…”. The extracted references also contain many apparent misspellings and malformed DOI or URL strings.

findings.recommendation: Perform a full copyedit against the source document: correct grammar and spelling, standardize hyphenation and bullet formatting, restore missing spaces, and verify every author name, journal title, DOI, and URL before printing.

findings.finding: Core scientific sections are incomplete for a poster that presents an evidence review and implementation model: there is no explicit methods section and no clearly delineated results or evidence-synthesis section.

evidence.description: The poster includes Abstract, background/problem sections, a case example, implications, framework, Conclusion, and References. The extracted headings do not include Methods or Results, even though the abstract says evidence and implementation models were examined and the PRACTICe section reports early outcomes.

findings.recommendation: Add explicit “Methods” and “Findings” or “Results” sections tailored to a narrative evidence review. State what was reviewed and then summarize the resulting evidence separately from interpretation and recommendations.

findings.finding: Citation numbering and reference details appear inconsistent, making source verification difficult.

evidence.description: Body text cites sources 1 through 15, but only reference 1 and references 10–15 visibly carry numbers in the extracted reference list; the intervening entries are unnumbered. Several citations contain malformed links or bibliographic text, including “https:/wwwwilda gow,” “ener 23157,” “Mips:/ncats. nih. gov,” and inconsistent naming of PRACTICe/PROCTICe.

findings.recommendation: Rebuild the reference list from verified source records, number every entry consecutively to match in-text citations, use one citation style consistently, and test all DOI and web links. Confirm the program name and acronym against the cited source.

findings.finding: Acronyms and specialist terminology increase the reading burden for viewers outside clinical-trial operations.

evidence.description: CROs and PCPs are expanded in early prose, but later sections use PBRNs, CTSA, WWAMI, ACRP, and NIH CARE for Health without providing all expansions or explanations. Terms such as “screen failure,” “upstream feasibility,” “role-limited engagement,” and “late-stage recruitment rescue” are also used without plain-language clarification.

findings.recommendation: Define every acronym at first use and replace or briefly explain specialist terms. A small glossary is preferable only if the terms cannot be removed.

findings.finding: The poster identifies the author and company but does not show visible contact information or an acknowledgement or disclosure statement.

evidence.description: The header reads “ROSA SWEENEY, MPH THERMO FISHER SCIENTIFIC.” No email address, QR code, acknowledgement, funding statement, or conflict-of-interest disclosure is present in the extracted content.

findings.recommendation: If appropriate for the meeting and organizational policy, add a contact email or QR code and a concise acknowledgement, funding, and conflict-of-interest statement. Contact information is an optional enhancement under the supplied checklist, not an asserted institutional requirement.
